aliases: Shulchan Aruch of Rabbi Joseph Karo

date.note: First printed at Venice in 1565 (compiled by Joseph Karo, 1488-1575). The work is arranged in four parts (turim), following the fourfold division of Jacob ben Asher's earlier Arbaah Turim: Orach Chayim, Yoreh Deah, Even ha-Ezer, and Choshen Mishpat. The Ashkenazi glosses of Moses Isserles (the Mappah, 'the Tablecloth') were composed and printed alongside the text from the Cracow editions onward (from 1569-1571); the openly-auditable Hebrew on Sefaria for Orach Chayim is the Maginei Eretz edition (Lemberg, 1893).

summary: The Shulchan Aruch ('The Set Table'), first printed at Venice in 1565, is the code of Jewish law compiled by Joseph Karo as a concise practical digest of his larger commentary the Beit Yosef, arranged in four parts (Orach Chayim, Yoreh Deah, Even ha-Ezer, Choshen Mishpat). Printed together with the Ashkenazi glosses of Moses Isserles, known as the Mappah ('the Tablecloth'), the combined work came to be regarded across both Sephardic and Ashkenazi communities as the central code of halakha.
description:
The Shulchan Aruch ('The Set Table' or 'The Prepared Table') is the code of Jewish law compiled by Joseph Karo (1488-1575), first printed at Venice in 1565. Karo composed it as a concise, practical digest distilled from his own far larger work, the Beit Yosef ('House of Joseph'), a comprehensive commentary on the Arbaah Turim of Jacob ben Asher in which he traced each ruling back through its sources. Where the Beit Yosef sets out the debate and its authorities at length, the Shulchan Aruch states the resulting ruling in brief, arranged for practical reference; on Karo's own account in his introduction it was written so that its rulings could be reviewed regularly and known by heart. The account that follows presents the work's structure, method, and standing as attributed features of the text and its reception in the tradition, not as claims the editor affirms.

The work follows the fourfold division of the earlier Arbaah Turim into four parts, each a tur ('row', as of the stones of the priestly breastplate): Orach Chayim ('the Path of Life'), on daily conduct, prayer, Sabbath, and the festivals; Yoreh Deah ('It Shall Teach Knowledge'), on dietary law, ritual purity, mourning, and a wide range of prohibitions; Even ha-Ezer ('the Stone of Help'), on marriage, divorce, and family law; and Choshen Mishpat ('the Breastplate of Judgment'), on civil and monetary law and the courts. Within each part the material is divided into numbered chapters (simanim) and sub-sections (seifim), producing a fine-grained reference apparatus. The opening ruling of Orach Chayim sets the tone of a practical digest of conduct: 'One should strengthen himself like a lion to get up in the morning to serve his creator', a formulation drawn from the counsel of Judah ben Tema in Pirkei Avot as mediated through the Tur.

Karo's method of decision, stated in his introduction to the Beit Yosef and carried into the Shulchan Aruch, was to follow, as a general rule, the ruling agreed by the majority of three earlier authorities he took as pillars: Isaac Alfasi (the Rif), Maimonides (the Rambam), and Asher ben Yehiel (the Rosh), deciding with the majority among them where they differed. This procedure reflected the Sephardic and broadly Mediterranean tradition in which Karo worked, and its rulings did not always match the customs of Ashkenazi communities. For that reason Moses Isserles of Cracow (the Rema, c. 1530-1572) added his glosses, collectively called the Mappah ('the Tablecloth', set over Karo's 'Set Table'), recording where Ashkenazi practice and later authorities differed and supplying the rulings customary among Ashkenazim. Isserles' gloss on the very first ruling of Orach Chayim illustrates the register of the combined work: to Karo's charge to rise like a lion he adds the verse 'I have set the Lord always before me' (Psalm 16:8), calling it 'a great principle in the Torah' and citing the discussion of the constant awareness of God in Maimonides' Guide of the Perplexed (III:52).

Because the two were printed together, Karo's rulings interleaved with Isserles' glosses, the combined Shulchan Aruch spoke to both major branches of practice at once, the base text carrying the Sephardic ruling and the Mappah the Ashkenazi, and it came in the reception of the tradition to be treated as the central and authoritative code of halakha, drawing in turn a vast literature of commentary and super-commentary around it. This entry describes that standing as the position it holds within the tradition and in the work's reception; it does not itself rule the code binding, and it attributes the code's authority to how it has been received rather than adjudicating it.
editorial_notes: This entry presents the Shulchan Aruch on Judaism's own terms as the halakhic code compiled by Joseph Karo and first printed at Venice in 1565, together with the Mappah glosses of Moses Isserles (neutrality #1, #4, #6). Its structure (four parts: Orach Chayim, Yoreh Deah, Even ha-Ezer, Choshen Mishpat), its origin as a digest of Karo's Beit Yosef, Karo's majority-of-three method (Alfasi, Maimonides, Asher), and the Ashkenazi Mappah are DESCRIBED as attributed features of the text and its reception, not adjudicated. NEUTRALITY: the code's authoritative status is stated as the standing it HOLDS WITHIN THE TRADITION and in its reception ('came to be regarded', 'came in the reception of the tradition to be treated as', 'attributes the code's authority to how it has been received'); the editor does NOT call it binding in its own voice. Sources triangulate per neutrality #8-#9: (a) the PRIMARY text on Sefaria, open and auditable, Orach Chayim 1:1 READ LINE-BY-LINE; (b) an academic monograph, R. J. Zwi Werblowsky, Joseph Karo: Lawyer and Mystic (Oxford, 1962); and (c) a contemporary Jewish scholar on-topic, Isadore Twersky, 'The Shulhan 'Aruk: Enduring Code of Jewish Law' (Judaism, 1967). No encyclopedias (no Encyclopaedia Judaica, no YIVO), no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources.
